During group projects and college activities, I often have to remind teammates about tasks, coordinate meeting timings, and keep track of deadlines. These things are important, but they can take up a lot of time. I would rather use that time to focus on the actual work, like analysing the problem, coming up with ideas, and making decisions. column24:
One task that made me feel quite frustrated was trying to understand and compare investment options for my own savings. I was looking at mutual funds, fixed deposits and insurance plans online, but every website used different terms and showed different returns. I remember spending a lot of time comparing things like returns, lock-in periods, charges and risks, but I still wasn't sure which option actually made sense for me.

What made it more confusing was that some plans sounded attractive because of the returns they advertised, but when I looked deeper, there were conditions and charges that were not obvious at first. I ended up making an Excel sheet to compare the options side by side and understand where my money would actually go.

It was a small task, but it made me realise how difficult financial products can feel when the information is not presented simply.
column25:
Right now, my system is fairly simple. I keep track of my expenses through my bank and UPI apps and try to review them at the end of the month. For investments, I usually discuss options with my family and do some research on my own before making a decision. I also use online platforms to compare mutual funds, fixed deposits, and other investment options rather than depending completely on one person.

For insurance, my family mainly handles the existing policies, and I am slowly trying to understand the details myself. I would not say that I have a perfect system yet. Sometimes I delay checking my finances or rely too much on recommendations from people I trust. But I am becoming more conscious about tracking where my money goes and making decisions after understanding the risks and benefits.

One task that has been difficult for me is staying consistent with exercise during busy college weeks. I remember having a week with classes, assignments and group work where I planned to go to the gym in the evening. By the time my classes and work were finished, I was tired and kept postponing it to the next day. After a few days, I realised I had not exercised at all.

The frustrating part was that I did want to stay active, but my schedule kept changing and I was treating exercise as something I would do only when I had free time. It made me realise that fitness is less about motivation and more about building a routine that actually fits into my day.
column40:

The difficult part is staying consistent when classes, assignments and group work get busy. I do not have a strict routine yet, so some weeks are much better than others. I usually rely on myself and occasionally discuss fitness or diet with my friends and family. I am still figuring out a system that is realistic enough for me to follow regularly rather than something that looks good on paper but is difficult to maintain.

I started an online course and was quite motivated in the beginning. But once classes, assignments and group projects became busy, I kept postponing the course.

I would open the course thinking I would spend 30 minutes learning, but then something else would come up. After a few weeks, I realised I had completed much less than I had planned. The frustrating part was that I was genuinely interested in the topic; the problem was being consistent. It made me realise that learning something new requires a routine and small, regular efforts rather than waiting for a completely free day.

I would say my system is still a work in progress. I learn a lot, but consistency is something I am trying to improve.

column2: The daily financial annoyance I want to rewire is the chaotic process of tracking cross-platform peer-to-peer settlements. While single apps split bills easily on the spot, reality is messy because friends pay you back using different methods over delayed timelines—one via GPay, another through Amazon Pay, and a third in cash. This remains unautomated because current payment apps operate in closed loops; they cannot reconcile transactions across competing platforms. I want to build an autonomous agent that securely tracks multi-channel financial notifications, intelligently links incoming cross-platform transfers back to the original split expense, and automatically reminds the specific friends who forgot to pay.

column24:
When it comes to money, investing, and insurance, I find it frustrating to choose the right option. There are so many insurance plans and investment products in the market, and every one of them has its own advantages and disadvantages. With insurance, I have to collect different quotations, compare coverage, exclusions, premiums, and benefits, and then make a decision. Having more choices gives us more opportunities, but it also creates more confusion and anxiety.

I experienced something similar when I was planning to invest in digital gold. My research suggested that gold prices were already high and could fall in the future, so I chose digital silver instead because the market trends showed strong growth. But later, silver prices started falling while gold continued to rise. It was frustrating to realize that even after spending so much time researching and studying investment strategies, the outcome could still be completely different.

The more choices we have, the more time and energy we spend trying to make the “right” decision and sometimes we still don't know whether it was the right one.

There are so many different apps, policies, and financial products available today. While having more choices gives us more opportunities, it also makes the decision-making process much more complicated.

Shopping and finding the best deals can be surprisingly difficult. Like everyone else, I always want to get things at the lowest possible price. When shopping online, the same or similar products can be available on different platforms at very different prices, so I have to compare multiple websites before deciding where to buy.

My grandma was unwell and I was in Gurugram. He was in Telangana.

The doctor asked for his previous reports. They were scattered across
three places: a folder at home nobody could find, a WhatsApp forward
from six months ago buried under 3,000 messages, and one physical
paper that my mother was holding in her hand but could not read
because it was in English.

I spent 45 minutes on a call, directing my family to scroll, search,
and photograph documents while I tried to piece together his medical
history in real time.

The doctor waited.

We found most of it. Not all of it.

The frustrating part was not the distance. It was that every single
report existed somewhere. Nothing was lost. It was just scattered,
unreadable, and impossible to find fast when it actually mattered.
column19:
My system is my mother.

She remembers every doctor's name, every medicine, every follow-up
date, and every report that was ever generated in our family. She
carries it all in her head because there is nowhere else to put it.

When something happens, I call her first. She tells me which doctor
we saw last time, what he said, and which folder the reports might
be in. Then I call the doctor. Then I call my father to find the
folder. Then I call my mother again to translate what the report says.

The system works because she has never forgotten anything in 25 years.

It will break the day she is the one who is unwell.

That is the part that keeps me up at night. The entire medical memory
of our family lives in one person, with no backup, no index, and no
way to hand it off.

column51: So last week I was heading back to my hostel from college, and I just needed to book an auto. Simple enough, right? I open the app, it shows me a 3 min wait, decent fare. Cool. But then out of habit I open another app just to check if it's cheaper, and it is, like ₹15 less, but the driver's like 12 minutes away. So now I'm sitting there actually debating whether ₹15 is worth waiting an extra 9 minutes for. While I'm doing this very important calculation, the first app's ETA jumps to 9 minutes anyway. So I cancel that one, book the "cheaper" one, and literally a minute later the driver cancels on me. Now I'm back to square one, both apps open, re-checking fares again, and I've probably burned like 8-10 minutes just trying to book a ride that should've taken 10 seconds. And this isn't even a one-off thing — this basically happens every single time I need to go from college to my hostel.
column52: Honestly, it's just me, bouncing between two or three apps every single time. I don't stick to one — I've got the auto app, a cab app, and sometimes I'll just check both before deciding. There's no real system, it's more like a reflex at this point: open app one, check fare, open app two, compare, panic slightly if the ETA changes, cancel, rebook, repeat. If it's late at night or I'm in a rush, I skip the comparing and just book whatever shows up fastest — but then I always have that nagging feeling I overpaid. No family involvement, no driver I call directly, no broker — just me, my phone, and way too many tabs open for something that should be a two-second decision.

- Creating a trip report online
- Entering activity, flight and hotel details
- Getting approvals
